title: Wait Time: Slowing Down May Be a Way of Speeding Up https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/epdf/10.1177/002248718603700110
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Tips for Teachers research summary covers Mary Budd Rowe's landmark, decades-spanning body of research on 'wait time' — the pause a teacher leaves after asking a question (Wait Time 1) and after a student responds (Wait Time 2). Rowe's central finding, replicated across more than 20 years of classroom study, is that extending both pauses to three seconds or more substantially improves the quality of classroom talk: longer and more evidence-based student responses, more student-initiated questions, more student-to-student interaction, and fewer discipline problems. The effect runs in both directions — longer wait time changes teachers too, producing more flexible teaching styles, fewer discourse errors, and higher-level questioning focused on clarification and elaboration rather than simple recall. Rowe found the second pause, Wait Time 2 (after the student answers, before the teacher reacts), has an even larger impact on outcomes than the first. She also identified a specific verbal habit — mimicking or echoing student answers — that quietly erodes wait time without teachers realising it, and found the benefits extend particularly to students with special educational needs, both gifted and those with more significant needs. Barton's summary frames longer wait time as a low-cost, high-leverage lever: counterintuitively, slowing down the pace of questioning speeds up the depth and quality of student thinking.
points: Extending both Wait Time 1 (after asking) and Wait Time 2 (after a student answers) to three seconds or more reliably improves response length, use of evidence and logic, and student-to-student interaction.
Wait Time 2 — the pause after a student responds, before the teacher reacts — has a larger effect on outcomes than Wait Time 1, making it the higher-leverage of the two pauses to train.
Longer wait time changes teacher behaviour too: more flexible responses, fewer discourse errors, and a shift toward higher-level, clarification-focused questioning rather than simple recall checks.
A specific, often-unnoticed habit — teachers mimicking or echoing student answers — actively erodes wait time, giving teachers a concrete behaviour to self-monitor and correct.

Extended wait time (especially Wait Time 1) particularly benefits students with special educational needs, including both gifted students and those with mild or severe handicaps, and is also associated with easier behaviour management.
quotes: Wait time refers to the amount of time teachers pause after asking a question and after students respond.

Rowe's research, spanning over 20 years, demonstrates that increasing wait times to 3 seconds or more significantly enhances the quality of student responses, promotes student engagement, and fosters deeper learning.
Teachers should aim for an average wait time of 3 seconds or more after asking a question (Wait Time 1) and after a student responds (Wait Time 2).
Longer wait times can also positively affect teachers: teachers' responses become more flexible and exhibit fewer discourse errors.
Teachers should be aware of verbal habits, such as mimicry (repeating student responses), that can inhibit longer wait times.
Extending wait time, particularly Wait Time 1, has also been shown to benefit students with special needs, including those who are gifted and those with mild or severe handicaps.
Research suggests that Wait Time 2 (pausing after a student's response) has a more significant impact on many outcomes.
